newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: U.S. development chief says Africa must liberalise.
newsitem.headline: U.S. development chief says Africa must liberalise.

text.p: U.S. development chief Brian Atwood warned African nations on Monday that liberalising their economies was the only way to cash in on a new U.S. economic plan for the world's most impoverished continent.

Atwood, director of the U.S. Agency for International Development, said many African governments still interfered too much with their economies and would find attracting foreign investment and boosting exports difficult.

"We are focusing on those countries that wish to reform their economies...it is impossible to work with a government that does not want to pursue market economics," he said on a video linkup from Washington to Johannesburg.
Last month U.S. President Bill Clinton launched an economic programme for Africa called "Partnership for Economic Growth and Opportunity".

Under the plan 1,800 more products from the poorest nations in Africa would receive duty-free access to the United States while nations undertaking concerted economic reform would benefit from reduced tariffs.
Two funds are also to be set up with a $150 million equity fund to increase private investment and a $500 million fund for infrastructure investment.

After the so-called "Lost Decade" of the 1980s, Africa is desperate to attract foreign interest. A wave of reform has swept away many of the state-oriented policies that have dominated the continent in the post-colonial era.

Notable successes include double-digit growth in once strife-ridden Uganda, in Ethiopia and in Zambia, which has gone from a rigid system of economic control to one of the most ambitious privatisation schemes in Africa.
But Atwood said African nations would have to reform yet further and be prepared to swallow tough medicine in the form of government spending cuts.
"There will be a period of time, it is clear, when many African countries will have to go through a period of pain," he said.

But Atwood added that the developed world should reward countries taking on much-needed austerity programmes with support in health and education. "That is where the international community comes into play," he said.
Africa faces enormous social problems with often struggling education systems, the AIDS epidemic and a healthcare network that still sees one in 16 African women die in childbirth.
The continent has also been riven by ethnic conflict, with bloodshed in Rwanda, Burundi and the former Zaire rarely away from the world's headlines.
Atwood said granting greater autonomy to regions within each country was the way forward to create a stable environment that would sustain growth and attrcat investment.
"Providing a great deal of local autonomy is both the best way to deal with potential ethnic conflict as well as to deal with development," he said.
